victoria-beckham-first-profit.headline: Victoria Beckham's fashion label posts first-ever profit after 18 years
victoria-beckham-first-profit.body_md:
Eighteen years, £69 million of cumulative losses, and — by her own account — more than one conversation with her husband about whether to just stop. On Monday, Victoria Beckham's fashion and beauty business posted its first-ever operating profit: £7.3 million for 2025, on revenues up 15% to £129.8 million.

It is a small number by the standards of the luxury houses her label has spent two decades trying to sit alongside. But for a company that lost money in every single year since Beckham founded it in 2008 — including a £1.6 million loss as recently as 2024 — it marks the point where the business stops being an extension of her husband's earning power and starts standing on its own.

![Victoria Beckham in 2018](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a8/VictoriaBeckham2018-2-Crop.jpg)

## The bill David paid

The Beckham name has always done double duty as marketing and as balance sheet. Victoria Beckham Holdings Ltd went, in the company's own later description, "tens of millions into the red" over its first decade and a half, burning through funding rounds and a 2017 investment that saw NEO Investment Partners take a 30% stake for £30 million. Sir David Beckham, whose post-playing career of sponsorships, punditry and the Inter Miami ownership stake has made him one of football's highest earners, repeatedly put money in to cover shortfalls and payroll — support that outside filings and reporting have pointed to since at least 2016.

That kind of subsidy is not unusual in celebrity fashion — plenty of famous-name labels exist as vanity projects or marketing vehicles that never need to clear a profit test on their own. What makes the Beckham case notable is the scale and duration of the losses relative to the eventual payoff, and the fact that the company kept going long enough to find one.

## What actually turned it around

The swing to profit was not driven by the clothes that built the brand's reputation. It came from beauty. Victoria Beckham Beauty, launched in 2019, now generates roughly two-thirds of group revenue, and its breakout product — a £104 Foundation Drops formula — sold out on launch and built a waitlist reported at more than 25,000 customers before restocking in 2026. Skincare sales more than doubled on the back of it. Sybille Darricarrère Lunel, who joined as chief executive in July 2025 from Christian Dior Couture, credited "several years of disciplined execution and strategic investment" rather than any single hit product.

It is the fifth consecutive year of double-digit revenue growth, and the company says momentum has carried into the first half of 2026. A permanent US store on Mercer Street in New York — housing fashion, beauty and fragrance under one roof — opens this month, the label's first real bet on brick-and-mortar retail in its largest growth market.

## The longer read

The arc here is less about Beckham herself than about what it actually costs to build a fashion house from nothing. Luxury brands with generations of capital and distribution behind them — the LVMHs and Kerings of the world — took decades to become what they are; a celebrity name buys attention on day one but not the infrastructure, wholesale relationships or manufacturing scale that make a label self-sustaining. Beckham's business needed 18 years and a beauty line, not a runway show, to get there. "After 20 years, people don't look at my brand as a celebrity brand anymore," she said of the milestone — a line that only makes sense once the accounts back it up.

The next test is whether beauty's momentum can fund the fashion side properly, rather than simply covering for it, and whether the New York store translates a media moment — the Beckhams' Netflix documentary, released last October, brought a fresh wave of attention — into repeat retail custom rather than a one-off spike.

man-city-enzo-fernandez-talks.headline: Manchester City open talks with Chelsea over £120m+ Enzo Fernandez transfer
man-city-enzo-fernandez-talks.body_md:
Manchester City have opened formal talks with Chelsea over a transfer for Enzo Fernandez, with the two clubs discussing a fee in the region of €140m (£120m+) as the summer window closes on Tuesday night. The Argentina midfielder has verbally agreed personal terms with City, according to Fabrizio Romano, though the deal still hinges on the clubs agreeing a number — Chelsea's asking price and City's opening moves have not yet converged.

![Enzo Fernández playing for Chelsea](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cc/Enzo_Fern%C3%A1ndez.jpg)

What makes the pursuit notable is not just the size of the fee but the identity of the man pushing for it. Enzo Maresca, who signed Fernandez's biggest admirer in himself while managing Chelsea, left Stamford Bridge in June to succeed Pep Guardiola at City after Guardiola stepped down at the end of last season. Xabi Alonso, appointed in May and in the Chelsea dugout since July, now finds one of his manager's most influential midfielders being courted by the very predecessor who developed him.

## A reunion three years in the making

Fernandez joined Chelsea from Benfica in January 2023 for a British transfer record of £106.8m (€121m), a fee that triggered his release clause after a World Cup-winning tournament with Argentina in Qatar. He has since added the 2024 Copa America to his medal collection and made himself a Chelsea mainstay — 118 Premier League appearances, 19 goals, 15 assists across three and a half seasons. That a club spent that kind of money less than four years ago and is now willing to let the player go says less about Fernandez's form than about the churn in Chelsea's dugout: Graham Potter, Mauricio Pochettino, Maresca and now Alonso have all taken charge since BlueCo's takeover, each with their own view of what the midfield should look like.

Alonso has been diplomatic in public. "Enzo is a good professional. He's training well," the Spaniard said last week, after Fernandez was left out of Chelsea's Carabao Cup squad — a decision the club has described as tactical rather than a sign the player is being frozen out. Chelsea have been lining up cover regardless, with Bournemouth's Alex Scott and Roma's Manu Kone among names under consideration should Fernandez leave.

For City, the move fits a broader midfield rebuild forced by departures on Guardiola's watch and after it: Rodri to Barcelona, Bernardo Silva out of contract, Nico Gonzalez to Newcastle. Elliot Anderson and Ayyoub Bouaddi have already arrived this summer; a player Maresca knows intimately, and trusts to run a game the way he wants it run, would be the marquee addition to sit alongside them.

Whether it happens by Tuesday's 11pm deadline is the immediate question. The bigger one — whether Chelsea's revolving cast of coaches can hold onto its record signings for longer than a manager's tenure — will outlast the window.

uk-prison-in-cell-capacity.headline: England's prisons to get more in-cell capacity as overcrowding crisis deepens
uk-prison-in-cell-capacity.body_md:
England's prison estate is, in the words of one former Conservative justice secretary, running "red hot" — and the new government's answer, for now, is not to pour concrete for new jails but to find spare rooms in the ones it already has.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris told MPs this week that £110m fast-tracked from existing budgets will go toward converting unused office space, laundry rooms and storage areas inside current prisons into cells, adding hundreds of places faster than any new-build programme could manage. It builds on more than 3,200 places already delivered over the past two years and sits alongside a 1,700-place prison under contract in Lancashire, part of a wider pledge to add 14,000 spaces by 2031.

![Watchtower at HMP Manchester, known as Strangeways](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/84/Strangeways_watchtower.jpg)

> In one sentence: The Ministry of Justice is retrofitting cells into existing prisons rather than building new ones, as Andy Burnham is warned that running the system near full capacity is a "big risk".

## A system with nowhere left to put people

England and Wales's prison population has pushed past 87,000, against a certified normal capacity of roughly 70,000 — a gap that has forced emergency measures since last spring, including police-cell overspill and an early-release scheme for thousands of prisoners nearing the end of their sentences. That scheme, reduced from around 6,000 to roughly 5,000 releases after ministers exempted rapists and serious child sexual offenders, is due to restart in October.

David Gauke, the former Tory minister who led the Starmer government's independent sentencing review, used a newspaper interview to warn that Prime Minister Andy Burnham — who took over from Keir Starmer in July — is "taking a big risk on prison capacity" by continuing to run the estate near its ceiling. Gauke said he understood Burnham was "in a bind", but described the stresses of operating at such tight margins as liable to produce exactly the kind of crunch that triggered emergency releases in the first place.

## Retrofit over new-build

The £110m announcement is notable less for its size — modest next to the multibillion-pound new-prison programme already under way — than for what it signals about sequencing. Building a prison from scratch takes years and planning permission; carving cells out of an existing laundry room or admin block can be done in months. For a government under fiscal pressure and needing capacity now rather than in 2031, that trade-off looks close to unavoidable.

Norris framed the investment as evidence of momentum rather than retreat: "This Government is serious about fixing the broken prison system we inherited... we're now investing to boost these efforts further, getting spades in the ground quicker to deliver thousands more places." The department is also directing money toward deporting foreign national offenders and considering earlier release for some prisoners serving indeterminate IPP sentences — both aimed at trimming the population rather than expanding the estate.

## What's next

The early-release scheme resumes in October, the next real test of whether the retrofitted capacity buys enough headroom to avoid another round of emergency measures. Gauke's review — and his public unease — suggests the sentencing side of the equation remains as contested as the building side.

badenoch-shadow-cabinet-reshuffle.headline: Badenoch reshuffles shadow cabinet, elevating Griffith and Tugendhat
badenoch-shadow-cabinet-reshuffle.body_md:
Kemi Badenoch spent Sunday doing what opposition leaders do best in the doldrums of a parliament: rearranging the furniture. The Conservative leader tore up her top team, installing Andrew Griffith as shadow chancellor in place of Sir Mel Stride and handing the foreign affairs brief to Tom Tugendhat, who replaces Dame Priti Patel. Sir James Cleverly, meanwhile, walked out of the shadow cabinet altogether — not into obscurity, but into a bid to become the Conservative candidate for Mayor of London.

![Official portrait of Kemi Badenoch](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d5/Official_portrait_of_Kemi_Badenoch_MP_crop_2%2C_2024.jpg)

**In one sentence:** Badenoch reshuffled her top team ahead of conference, promoting Griffith and Tugendhat and losing Cleverly to a London mayoral bid — a management story, not a policy one.

## Out with the old guard

Stride departs after nearly two years shadowing the Treasury, a stint Conservative aides credited with helping the party "rebuild economic credibility" after the Truss-era mini-Budget wrecked it. Patel, one of the more recognisable faces of the Boris Johnson years, returns to the backbenches with what allies describe as a new international role rather than a demotion in name only. Stuart Andrew also lost his health brief to Damian Hinds. None of the outgoing trio are gone from frontline politics for good, but all three lose the shadow cabinet table.

Griffith's promotion is the more pointed of the two headline moves, if only because of the baggage he carries. He was a Treasury minister under Liz Truss during the 2022 mini-Budget that triggered a gilt-market rout and ended her premiership in weeks — a fact Labour's Bridget Phillipson was quick to weaponise, branding him "a key architect of Liz Truss's disastrous mini-Budget." Griffith's response was to lean into ambition rather than apologise for the past, promising an "economic revolution" built on lower taxes, deregulation and more domestic oil and gas production.

## Tugendhat's second act

Tugendhat, a former army officer and one-time leadership rival to Badenoch, moves from security-adjacent portfolios to shadow foreign secretary — a natural enough fit given his years chairing the Commons foreign affairs select committee. Patel's exit from that brief closes out a period in which she had become a familiar voice on immigration and asylum policy; her successor is expected to bring a more Atlanticist, defence-minded tone to the role, though the party has given no indication of a substantive shift in foreign policy positioning.

Claire Coutinho steps up to shadow business secretary, taking the slot Griffith vacates, while Katie Lam moves into the housing brief left empty by Cleverly's departure.

## Cleverly's exit, and why it matters more for London than Westminster

Of the three big personnel changes, Cleverly's is the one with the clearest immediate consequence — just not for national politics. In a piece for The Times announcing his move, the former home and foreign secretary wrote that London's capital "needs more than an administrator," and told Badenoch he had to be "free to speak about every aspect of London's future" to make a real run at City Hall. He has since launched his campaign on a "classically Conservative" platform of tougher policing, more housebuilding and lower taxes — though Londoners will not actually choose a mayor until May 2028, leaving a long selection race ahead among party members.

## The bit that isn't there

What the reshuffle does not contain is any hint of a rethink on fiscal or monetary policy. Griffith's rhetoric about tax cuts and deregulation is standard opposition fare, not a costed platform, and nothing in the appointments touches the party's actual positioning on gilts, spending rules or the Bank of England. The move reads as pure party management: Badenoch shoring up her authority and refreshing a top team before October's conference, at a moment when polling puts the Conservatives in third place — trailing both Labour and a resurgent Reform UK, which recent surveys have shown a few points ahead of the Tories. For a party fighting to be heard at all, getting faces right matters more than getting policy right, at least for now.

The next marker to watch is the Conservative conference itself in October, where Griffith will face his first real test of turning "economic revolution" rhetoric into something resembling a platform — and where the party's polling position, not its cabinet lineup, will do the talking.

child-trust-fund-review.headline: Child trust fund providers face review over £1.5bn in unclaimed pots
child-trust-fund-review.body_md:
It began as one of New Labour's tidier ideas: give every child born after September 2002 a £250 government voucher, lock it into an investment account, and let compound growth do the rest of the work by the time they turned 18. Two decades on, a sizeable chunk of that money is still sitting there, unclaimed, and the Financial Conduct Authority wants to know why the firms holding it haven't tried harder to give it back.

The regulator has written to all 55 providers still running child trust funds, asking them to account for their efforts to trace customers who have lost touch with their accounts. Roughly 760,000 pots, worth an average of £2,000 each, remain unclaimed — a total of about £1.5bn spread across the cohort born between September 2002 and January 2011, who are now aged 15 to 23. The FCA says it will press harder on providers with large market shares or "potential indicators of consumer harm," and report back next year.

![Piggy bank](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e4/Piggy_bank.jpg)

## A scheme built to be forgotten

Child trust funds were, by design, easy to lose track of. Some 6.3 million children were enrolled before the scheme closed to new entrants in 2011, and a meaningful slice of those accounts were opened automatically by HM Revenue & Customs on behalf of parents who never filled in the paperwork — often because the child was in care, or the family simply missed the window. Those accounts drifted through address changes, teenage years and university moves with nobody actively managing them or, in many cases, even aware they existed.

The FCA's review found that only four of the 55 providers have voluntarily joined a shared tracing register run by the Tracing Group, a commercial outfit that has managed to map around 60% of all child trust funds. The rest have shown, in the regulator's words, little enthusiasm for making the search easier. That gap has created an opening for claims-management firms, some of which have charged up to £400 — or ongoing subscriptions — to do what HMRC's own tracing tool does for free.

"You don't need to pay someone else to claim what's rightfully yours," said Chris Knight, the FCA's director of insurance. "Tracing and accessing your own child trust fund costs nothing."

## What happens next

HMRC has already started writing directly to 21-year-olds with unmatched accounts, using PAYE and student finance records to find current addresses — a tactic that trims the unclaimed pile but doesn't reach the youngest cohort, whose accounts won't mature until 2029. The Share Foundation, a charity that helps reunite people with their funds, wants the government to go further and automatically release money to account holders once they turn 21, arguing it could put more than £550m into young adults' hands, over a third of it to those from lower-income households.

For providers, the FCA's report next year is the date that matters: a finding of inadequate tracing efforts could trigger enforcement action and set a template for how firms are expected to handle other categories of dormant retail accounts, from old pensions to forgotten ISAs. For everyone else, the simplest step remains the one the regulator keeps repeating — check the free HMRC tracing tool before anyone offers to check it for a fee.

kushner-world-cup-regret.headline: Kushner expresses regret over shelved World Cup ticket sell-off plan
kushner-world-cup-regret.body_md:
The apology arrived a month late and from the wrong Kushner, in the strictest sense — though in the family business sense, exactly on schedule. Joshua Kushner, the venture capitalist brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared, broke his silence this week on the collapse of a plan that would have handed his firm a slice of the World Cup itself.

"Had we known what this would devolve into, we would not have gotten involved," Kushner said, in his first public comments since FIFA's so-called Forward Enterprise scheme blew up in July. "We failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football."

![Joshua Kushner at the 2026 Met Gala](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/1a/Guests_at_the_2026_Met_Gala_289_%28Joshua_Kushner%29.jpg)

## The deal that wasn't

The plan, unveiled by FIFA president Gianni Infantino in late July, was audacious even by football's recent standards of audacity. FIFA would bundle the commercial guts of the World Cup — broadcast rights, sponsorship, ticketing, licensing — into a new entity called FIFA Forward Enterprise, then sell a 20% stake to outside investors for as much as $4.2bn. Thrive Eternal, the fund founded by Kushner's Thrive Capital, was positioned as the lead buyer, valuing the new unit at around $20bn.

Infantino framed it as redistribution: the proceeds, he said, would lift funding for FIFA's 211 member associations from £5.9m to £14.7m over the 2027–2030 cycle. Kushner still defends that logic. "We stand behind the motivations of FFE," he said this week — the aim, in his telling, was simply to "direct more capital and equity equally" across the sport's poorer corners.

## Who killed it

Nobody in football bought the framing. UEFA's 55 members voted to boycott FIFA events over the plan within days, calling the World Cup "not an investment product" and accusing Infantino of undervaluing the tournament — UEFA put its worth closer to £15bn than the sum implied by FIFA's own numbers — while bypassing any competitive process. CONCACAF and the Asian confederation lined up alongside them. In Washington, House Judiciary Democrats piled on with a sharper political edge, casting the arrangement as a "kickback" that put FIFA into direct business with the Trump family. FIFA shelved the plan within days of it becoming public. UEFA has since sought subpoenas for testimony and documents from Kushner and Thrive, and is weighing a formal complaint against Infantino.

## What it leaves behind

For Kushner personally, the fallout looks more like a rounding error than a reckoning: less than a month after the FFE scheme died, he and former Disney chief Bob Iger struck a deal to buy the Los Angeles Lakers at a $12.5bn valuation. For FIFA and Infantino, the damage sits closer to the bone — a rare moment where the federation's own confederations turned on a monetisation scheme before it could be signed, sealed and spent.

The broader signal is the one worth sitting with as the World Cup itself approaches kickoff next June. Sports properties have spent two decades getting more comfortable selling equity stakes to outside capital — franchises, leagues, even hospitality rights. This was the moment a governing body tried to do it with the tournament's entire commercial core, and its own membership stopped it cold within a week. Whether that holds as a hard ceiling on privatisation, or just a badly timed pitch to the wrong investor at the wrong political moment, is the question UEFA's subpoenas may end up answering before the opening whistle does.
